content: A study conducted by C et al. in rural Zimbabwe explored the feasibility of using the GeneXpert platform for simultaneous testing of HIV and tuberculosis (TB). This research, published in PLOS One in 2018, highlighted the potential for integrated disease testing to improve diagnostic efficiency. Additionally, the Clinton Health Access Initiative has been preparing a report on the patient impact, programmatic benefits, and cost savings associated with integrated testing approaches. Since the release of the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention, rapid advancements in antiretroviral therapy (ART) implementation and emerging evidence have necessitated a review and update of service delivery guidelines. In late 2018, a scoping exercise was conducted with national HIV program managers, implementing partners, civil society representatives, and academics to identify priority questions for guideline updates. Subsequently, a virtual meeting of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) was held in October 2020, following WHO standards for guideline development. Fourteen systematic reviews were conducted to address specific PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions and to inform updates to definitions. These reviews were supplemented by targeted literature searches, programmatic data, and primary surveys. The guideline development process involved contributions from a diverse group, including people living with HIV, representatives of affected communities, health ministry officials, researchers, implementers, and healthcare providers. Evidence synthesis and recommendations were guided by the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology, which assesses the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The GRADE approach evaluates the certainty of evidence based on factors such as study design, risk of bias, precision, consistency, and magnitude of effect. Recommendations were formulated by weighing the desirable effects (e.g., improved health outcomes, reduced morbidity and mortality, cost savings) against undesirable effects (e.g., potential harms, implementation challenges, or inefficiencies). Good practice statements were developed when indirect evidence strongly supported a net benefit relative to harms, and when collecting additional evidence would be unnecessarily burdensome. These statements were also informed by equity and ethical considerations, ensuring that implementation would result in significant positive outcomes without being contested or deemed unethical. The guideline development process included the use of the PRECIS-2 tool to assess the pragmatic or explanatory nature of studies. Systematic reviews adhered to PRISMA guidelines for reporting, and feasibility and acceptability were evaluated using indirect evidence from systematic reviews, UNAIDS databases, and stakeholder insights. Between July and September 2020, two online surveys were conducted with healthcare workers, HIV program managers, and people living with HIV to assess the feasibility and acceptability of service delivery strategies. Additional surveys and focus group discussions were conducted to explore psychosocial support interventions for adolescents and youth. Resource use and cost-effectiveness were analyzed through systematic reviews capturing data on costs, affordability, and cost-effectiveness. National program representatives provided perspectives on resource implications in their respective countries. Ethical considerations were reviewed by a WHO expert in global health and ethics, with key equity issues presented to the GDG for consideration during recommendation formulation. The GDG met virtually from October 5–9, 2020, to update recommendations. Systematic review outcomes were ranked using the GRADE scale, and evidence-to-decision-making tables were prepared and shared in advance. Recommendations were made by consensus, with a pre-agreed threshold of two-thirds of votes required for decision-making if necessary. Good practice principles were formulated based on the group’s expertise and the absence of harm in the evidence base. Draft guidelines were reviewed by the GDG and an External Review Group, with comments incorporated into the final document. All contributors completed WHO declarations of interest forms, and potential conflicts of interest were reviewed and managed. A web-based search was conducted to identify competing interests, and results were shared with the WHO Guideline Steering Group. Any conflicts were disclosed at the start of the GDG meeting, and management plans were implemented as needed. One GDG member, who led a systematic review informing the meeting, was excluded from voting on the corresponding recommendation. No other conflicts warranted exclusion from discussions. The guideline development process adhered to WHO policies, ensuring transparency, inclusivity, and ethical rigor.
